item.title: Federal Real Property: Commerce Could Save Tens of Millions of Dollars by Consolidating Underused Office Space
item.description:
What GAO Found
Most of the Department of Commerce’s (Commerce) office space was underutilized in early 2026 when compared to the Utilizing Space Efficiently and Improving Technologies (USE IT) Act target of 60 percent utilization. Specifically, GAO found that about 59 percent of Commerce’s 351 office locations were underutilized across the department and its 13 bureaus. This is consistent with the General Services Administration’s (GSA) 2026 utilization report for Commerce over the same time period. In fiscal year 2025 Commerce spent over $220 million on underutilized office locations.
Example of Underutilized Space – Department of Commerce Headquarters
Commerce collected occupancy data for its largest offices using badge swipes, but most of its office locations reported using a daily check-in survey. However, some bureaus that reported using the daily survey method varied in how they collected occupancy data, and their procedures did not align with GSA’s guidelines. This has affected the accuracy of data collected at some office locations. For example, one bureau reported the number of employees assigned to an office rather than the number of employees physically in the office daily, which overstates the utilization rate. Without implementing survey procedures that align with GSA guidelines, Commerce may continue to provide inaccurate occupancy data for certain locations. This could lead to inaccurate decisions and unnecessary costs for underutilized office locations.
Commerce has some efforts underway to increase utilization, but it has not identified department-wide consolidation opportunities or incorporated them into its real property capital plan. The plan indicates that several bureaus have completed or plan to reduce space. However, GAO’s review of Commerce’s utilization data found that there are 10 metropolitan areas with multiple Commerce bureaus in underutilized office locations, where further consolidation might help the department meet the USE IT Act utilization target. Commerce’s space-matching program, which placed employees in spaces as they returned to the office after the pandemic, has shown that department-wide efforts can be successful. By incorporating a department-wide consolidation plan into its real property capital plan, Commerce would be better positioned to meet utilization requirements in more locations and potentially save tens of millions of dollars by further consolidating or eliminating its office locations.
Why GAO Did This Study
Managing federal real property has been on GAO’s High Risk List for 23 years. In 2023, GAO reported that Commerce and other federal agencies’ headquarters spaces were underutilized and costly. In 2025, Commerce implemented policy changes to bring employees back to the office full-time.
GAO was asked to review Commerce’s office space use nationwide. This report examines (1) the utilization of Commerce’s office space department-wide and the costs of that office space, (2) how Commerce collects occupancy data for its office space, and how that approach affects the accuracy of the data, and (3) the extent to which Commerce is addressing underutilization.
GAO analyzed Commerce’s USE IT Act data submissions for 351 office locations from January 12 through March 6, 2026. GAO calculated average daily utilization of each location by dividing its average daily occupancy over the period by the location’s capacity. GAO also reviewed Commerce real property guidance and summarized cost and collection method data for Commerce’s office space. GAO also visited Commerce office spaces to observe office layouts and use of space in the national capital region, Colorado, and Georgia. GAO selected these areas based on the variety of bureaus present and other factors. Lastly, GAO interviewed GSA and Commerce officials.
